steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on detecting propaganda techniques in code-switched (English and Roman Urdu) social media text, including why it matters and what we contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Social media, misinformation and propaganda
- Code-switching on social media; English + Roman Urdu
- Related code-switched NLP and propaganda detection work; the gap
- Challenges
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Propaganda on social media
  - social media changed how people consume/share information; easy to reach mass public
  - primary source of news, used daily
  - propaganda: biased/misleading info to manipulate beliefs and opinions towards an objective
  - always existed; social media makes spreading agendas fast and wide
  - harms: COVID-19 pandemic - wrong details about the virus and vaccine effectiveness -> confusion, mistrust
  - manipulates emotions/behaviour, political or ideological; weakens critical thinking and informed decisions
  - need to detect propaganda; more accurate, truthful exchange of information
- Code-switching
  - Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram; millions of users, many bilingual/multilingual
  - mixing languages in posts, tweets, comments, chats
  - code-switching = switching between languages in same context; within or across sentences
  - compensates for lack of proper expression; more accurate, convincing expression
  - our setting: English (high-resource) + Roman Urdu (low-resource; Urdu in Latin script)
  - Urdu has native script but Roman Urdu preferred online for typing convenience
  - Figure 1: example code-switched text with fragment-level propaganda labels
- Related work + gap
  - code-switched NLP: Language Identification, NER, POS Tagging, Sentiment Analysis, QA, NLI
  - little on propaganda detection, esp. low-resource languages
  - prior: English; document-level binary and multi-class; fragment-level on journalistic news articles
  - ours: first on code-switched low-resource languages on social media
- Challenges
  - no specific corpora, no high-quality reliable annotations, no fine-tuned models
- Contributions
  - 1. novel task: propaganda techniques in code-switched text
  - 2. new corpus: 1,030 English/Roman Urdu texts, fragment-level, 20 techniques
  - 3. experiments: monolingual, multilingual, cross-lingual models, LLMs; comparative analysis

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The rise of social media has significantly changed the way people consume and share information. With the Internet and the widespread use of social media platforms, it is now easier for anyone to spread information to the mass public. In the digital era social media platforms have become the main source of news consumption and people use them every day. One main way that falsified information is circulated is through propaganda. Propaganda is spreading biased or misleading information in order to manipulate people's beliefs and opinions towards a particular objective. Propaganda has always existed, but social media platforms have made it easier for individuals and organizations to push their agenda and narratives quickly to large audiences. Propaganda and the spread of misleading facts and opinions affect many people negatively and may cause harm. We saw this especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, when wrong details about the virus and about how effective vaccines are spread on social media platforms, and this led to confusion and mistrust among the public. Propaganda is also used as a tool to manipulate people's emotions and behavior, often for political or ideological purposes. This can lead to a decline in critical thinking, so people are less able to make well-informed decisions based on factual information and evidence. So there is a need to detect propaganda, to fight its negative effects and to promote a more accurate and truthful exchange of information on social media.

Social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram are used by millions of people around the world, and many of these users are bilingual or even multilingual. Because there are more multilingual users and interactions on social media are informal, a large number of people have started mixing multiple languages on social media platforms, in posts, tweets, comments, and especially chats. This is where the term code-switching comes from. Code-switching mainly means switching or alternating between multiple languages in the same context. The switch can happen within the same sentence or from one sentence to the next. This phenomenon of code-switching, or mixing multiple languages, is now prevalent on social media platforms among bilingual and multilingual communities. Switching languages makes up for a lack of proper expression. It helps people express their ideas and thoughts more accurately and convincingly, so they have a more meaningful impact on readers and listeners. In this work we want to detect propaganda techniques in code-switched text, and we use English and Roman Urdu (i.e., Urdu written in Latin script) as our high-resource and low-resource languages. Urdu has its own native script, but most people prefer Roman Urdu in their online text communication because it is more convenient to type. Figure 1 shows an example of code-switched text (English and Roman Urdu), where the different fragments of the text are labeled with propaganda techniques.

- Related work + gap
  - code-switched NLP tasks: Language Identification, NER, POS Tagging, Sentiment Analysis, QA, NLI
  - little propaganda detection, esp. low-resource; prior work English, document-level binary/multi-class, fragment-level news articles
  - ours: first on code-switched low-resource languages on social media
- Challenges: no corpora, no reliable annotations, no fine-tuned models
- Contributions
  - 1. novel task
  - 2. corpus: 1,030 English/Roman Urdu texts, fragment-level, 20 techniques
  - 3. monolingual, multilingual, cross-lingual models, LLMs; comparative analysis

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The rise of social media has significantly changed the way people consume and share information. With the Internet and the widespread use of social media platforms, it is now easier for anyone to spread information to the mass public. In the digital era social media platforms have become the main source of news consumption and people use them every day. One main way that falsified information is circulated is through propaganda. Propaganda is spreading biased or misleading information in order to manipulate people's beliefs and opinions towards a particular objective. Propaganda has always existed, but social media platforms have made it easier for individuals and organizations to push their agenda and narratives quickly to large audiences. Propaganda and the spread of misleading facts and opinions affect many people negatively and may cause harm. We saw this especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, when wrong details about the virus and about how effective vaccines are spread on social media platforms, and this led to confusion and mistrust among the public. Propaganda is also used as a tool to manipulate people's emotions and behavior, often for political or ideological purposes. This can lead to a decline in critical thinking, so people are less able to make well-informed decisions based on factual information and evidence. So there is a need to detect propaganda, to fight its negative effects and to promote a more accurate and truthful exchange of information on social media.

Social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram are used by millions of people around the world, and many of these users are bilingual or even multilingual. Because there are more multilingual users and interactions on social media are informal, a large number of people have started mixing multiple languages on social media platforms, in posts, tweets, comments, and especially chats. This is where the term code-switching comes from. Code-switching mainly means switching or alternating between multiple languages in the same context. The switch can happen within the same sentence or from one sentence to the next. This phenomenon of code-switching, or mixing multiple languages, is now prevalent on social media platforms among bilingual and multilingual communities. Switching languages makes up for a lack of proper expression. It helps people express their ideas and thoughts more accurately and convincingly, so they have a more meaningful impact on readers and listeners. In this work we want to detect propaganda techniques in code-switched text, and we use English and Roman Urdu (i.e., Urdu written in Latin script) as our high-resource and low-resource languages. Urdu has its own native script, but most people prefer Roman Urdu in their online text communication because it is more convenient to type. Figure 1 shows an example of code-switched text (English and Roman Urdu), where the different fragments of the text are labeled with propaganda techniques.

A lot of research has been done on different code-switched tasks in Natural Language Processing (NLP), such as Language Identification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), POS Tagging, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering, and Natural Language Inference (NLI). But propaganda detection has not been explored much, especially for low-resource languages. Previous work here has mostly focused on high-resource languages like English, with propaganda detection at the document level as both a binary-class and a multi-class classification task, and at the fragment level for journalistic news articles. Our research is the first attempt at propaganda detection in code-switched low-resource languages on social media, and detecting these texts has become vital for a healthier online environment. There are several challenges in this task though, including a lack of specific corpora, of high-quality and reliable annotations, and of fine-tuned models. Our approach tries to overcome these challenges by focusing on propaganda detection on social media platforms. Our contributions are as follows:

1. We formulate the new NLP task of detecting propaganda techniques in code-switched text.

2. We build and annotate a new corpus for this task, with 1,030 code-switched texts in English and Roman Urdu. The texts are annotated at the fragment level with 20 propaganda techniques.

3. We experiment with different model classes for this task and dataset, including monolingual, multilingual, cross-lingual models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), and we give a comparative performance analysis.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The rise of social media has brought about a significant change in the way people consume and share information. With the advent of the Internet and the widespread use of social media platforms, it has become easier for anyone to spread information to the mass public. In the digital era, social media platforms have become the primary source of news consumption and are used on a daily basis. One main method of circulating falsified information is propaganda. Propaganda is the dissemination of biased or misleading information in order to manipulate people's beliefs and opinions towards a particular objective. Propaganda has always existed, but social media platforms have made it easier for individuals and organizations to promote their agenda and narratives quickly across large audiences. Propaganda and the spread of misleading facts and opinions negatively affect many people and may cause harm. This was particularly visible during the COVID-19 pandemic, when incorrect details about the virus and the effectiveness of vaccines spread on social media platforms, leading to confusion and mistrust among the public. Propaganda is also used as a tool to manipulate people's emotions and behavior, often for political or ideological purposes. This can result in a decline in critical thinking abilities, impairing the capacity to make well-informed decisions grounded in factual information and evidence. Thus, there is a need to detect propaganda to combat its negative effects and to promote a more accurate and truthful exchange of information across social media.

Social media platforms such as Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and Instagram are used by millions of people around the world, and many of these users are bilingual or even multilingual. Due to the increase in multilingual users and informal interactions on social media, a large number of people have begun mixing multiple languages on various social media platforms in posts, tweets, comments, and especially chats. This is where the term code-switching comes from. Code-switching primarily refers to switching or alternating between multiple languages in the same context, either within the same sentence or from one sentence to the next. This phenomenon of code-switching has now become prevalent on social media platforms among bilingual and multilingual communities. This language alternation compensates for a lack of proper expression, helping individuals express their ideas and thoughts more accurately and convincingly and have a more meaningful impact on readers and listeners [1,2,3]. In this work, we aim to detect propaganda techniques in code-switched text: we use English and Roman Urdu (i.e., Urdu written using Latin script) as our high-resource and low-resource languages. Although Urdu has its native script, most individuals prefer Roman Urdu in their online textual communication due to the convenience of typing. Figure 1 shows an example of a code-switched text (English and Roman Urdu), where the different fragments of the text are labeled as propaganda techniques.

Significant research efforts have been dedicated to various code-switched tasks in Natural Language Processing (NLP), such as Language Identification, Named Entity Recognition (NER), POS Tagging, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering, and Natural Language Inference (NLI) [4,5,6,7]. However, propaganda detection has seen limited exploration, particularly for low-resource languages. Previous work in this area has focused mainly on high-resource languages such as English, with propaganda detection at the document level as both a binary-class and multi-class classification task [8,9], and at the fragment level for journalistic news articles [10]. Our research is the first attempt to address propaganda detection in code-switched low-resource languages on social media, where detecting these texts has become vital to create a healthier online environment. However, this task poses several challenges, including a lack of specific corpora, of high-quality and reliable annotations, and of fine-tuned models. Our approach aims to overcome these challenges by focusing on propaganda detection on social media platforms. We summarize the contributions of our work as follows:

- 1. We formulate the novel NLP task of detecting propaganda techniques in code-switched text.

- 2. We construct and annotate a new corpus for this task, comprising 1,030 code-switched texts in English and Roman Urdu, annotated at the fragment level with 20 propaganda techniques.

- 3. We experiment with various model classes, including monolingual, multilingual, cross-lingual models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), for this task and dataset, and provide a comparative performance analysis.
